source.title_on_document: The Application of Multimodal Generative AI in College English Creative Writing Instruction

supplement.holds: No supplementary file or appendix is identified. References occupy pp. 15-16 and Figures 1-6 occupy pp. 17-21 of this PDF. No source for the missing analyzed counts, group-specific results, or uncertainty statistics is supplied.

paper_design_summary: The paper describes an eight-week college creative-writing intervention involving 60 first-year non-English-major students, with 30 assigned to multimodal AI instruction and 30 to traditional instruction; it simultaneously calls the design quasi-experimental and says students were randomly assigned (p. 7, sections 3.2-3.3). Teachers evaluated writing, and the results present pretest/posttest language and creativity scores without identifying group-specific results or analyzed participant counts (pp. 8, 11-12). A nested image comparison reports 30 works analyzed, with student-image and AI-image source labels; who prompted the AI images and what assistance produced the student-image pool are not established (p. 10, section 4.2.4; pp. 12-13, section 5.2.2 and Table 5).

studies.label: College English creative-writing instruction, with nested image comparison

assignment.what_was_assigned: The paper explicitly says students were randomly assigned to experimental AI instruction or traditional instruction. field_rct, randomized=yes, and unit=individual record this literal claim provisionally; the same paragraph calls the design quasi-experimental and describes two natural classes. The actual allocation procedure and its relationship to class membership are not established (p. 7, section 3.2). structure=mixed reflects between-group instruction plus repeated pretest/posttest measurements (pp. 7-8).
assignment.quote: Using a quasi-experimental design, students are randomly assigned to an experimental group and a control group (30 each).
assignment.locator: p. 7, section 3.2; pp. 7-8, sections 3.3.1-3.3.4 (between-group instruction and repeated pretest/posttest measurements); p. 15, section 6.3

arms.name: Multimodal generative AI instruction
arms.description: Experimental instruction using ChatGPT, Midjourney and DALL·E for ideas, drafting, revision and visual expression with teacher guidance; assignment count is 30 (p. 7, section 3.2).

arms.name: Traditional instruction
arms.description: Conventional writing instruction, group brainstorming, independent drafting and teacher feedback/correction, without the experimental AI tools; assignment count is 30 (pp. 7-8, sections 3.2-3.3). This is ordinary teaching rather than a separate experimentally added aid.

participants.exclusions: No exclusions, attrition, completed-posttest denominator, or analyzed participant count is reported. The 60 students and 30 per group occur in the sampling/assignment description (p. 7, section 3.2). The procedural statement that all students submit final works (p. 8, section 3.3.3) does not report how many enter the analyses. Table 5 counts 30 works, not people (p. 13).
participants.who: First-year non-English-major university students in two natural classes at one university (p. 7, section 3.2; p. 15, section 6.3). Two teachers and one AI technical staff member support the study; they are not additional students producing the scored writing (p. 7, section 3.2).
participants.quote: The study targets 60 first-year non-English major university students (divided into two natural classes).
participants.locator: p. 7, section 3.2 (60 students and 30 per group); p. 8, sections 3.3-3.4; pp. 11-13, Tables 2, 4 and 5; p. 15, section 6.3

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT, Midjourney, DALL·E; model versions not stated (p. 7, section 3.2).
ai_tool.how_used: Teacher-guided student prompting for ideas, metaphors, outlines and draft text; iterative student revision and AI feedback; persona prompts; image generation from keywords or paragraphs, and multimodal presentation. The role also includes refinement and image generation (pp. 7-10, sections 3.2-3.3 and 4.2).

task.description: English poems, stories and prose on cultural narratives, ecological writing and identity themes; students create and revise texts and add images/multimodal presentations (pp. 7-10, sections 3.3 and 4.1-4.3). Table 5 additionally compares student-generated and AI-generated visual interpretations (p. 13).
task.duration: Eight weeks, 16 sessions, two per week; initiation in Weeks 1-2, practice in Weeks 3-6, presentation in Week 7 and evaluation in Week 8 (pp. 7-8, section 3.3). No per-writing-task time limit stated.

outcomes.name: Composite creativity score
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Torrance-framework scoring of AI-assisted texts is explicit (p. 12, section 5.2.1). General writing evaluations use two teachers, cross-validated with Grammarly/ChatGPT scoring tools (p. 8, section 3.4); separate teacher and AI scores are not reported. Table 4 gives pretest/posttest means without identifying the instructional group, analyzed student denominator, scored-text count, rubric range, or score aggregation. The observation contributing to each reported mean is unspecified: individual texts, participant aggregates, and individual ratings cannot be distinguished; unit=null (p. 8, section 3.5; pp. 11-12, Tables 2 and 4). with_ai and availability=yes follow the explicit AI-assisted-text description, not an assumption about the separate Week 8 posttests; the connection between those posttests and these scored texts remains unstated (p. 8, section 3.3.4). No AI-withdrawal assessment or delayed follow-up is established. No outcome is explicitly designated primary. The composite formula is not reported. It is ordered first by the codebook preference, not by an explicit primary-outcome designation. The conclusion gives different creativity values without explaining their relationship to Table 4 (p. 14, section 6.1).

outcomes.name: Overall writing-performance score
outcomes.measure_detail: Writing quality is scored on a 10-point scale using the College English Writing Evaluation Standards (2020); pretest/posttest writing themes are identical (p. 11, sections 5.1-5.1.1). General writing evaluation uses dual teacher scoring with AI cross-validation (p. 8, section 3.4). Table 2 reports means and improvements without instructional-arm labels, analyzed people/text counts, or uncertainty. The observation contributing to each reported mean is unspecified: individual texts, participant aggregates, and individual ratings cannot be distinguished; unit=null (p. 8, section 3.5; pp. 11-12, Tables 2 and 4). AI use during instruction is explicit, but availability while producing these particular test texts is not reported. question and ai_available_when_produced are therefore null; neither with_ai nor after_ai is established for these test scores. The conclusion separately claims a 12.6% writing increase while referring to the control group, without providing the corresponding arm means or explaining its relationship to Table 2 (p. 14, section 6.1).

outcomes.name: Image comparison: imagery complexity
outcomes.measure_detail: Table 5 reports Student Image Average and AI Image Average, without identifying randomized instructional arms (p. 13, section 5.2.2). Its N = 30 works analyzed counts outputs; source-specific counts, unique student contributors, and pairing are unstated. The image-specific rubric, scoring procedure, assessors, scale, and reliability are not identified; measure=null. Students generate images with DALL·E during instruction (p. 10, section 4.2.4), but the paper does not establish who prompted the Table 5 AI-image pool or whether AI assisted the student-image pool. The image-source labels therefore do not establish an AI-versus-human context comparison in which no person receives AI help. question, ai_available_when_produced, and comparison_type are null pending production details. Student work produced with image-generation assistance would answer with_ai for these non-diversity constructs. No separately recruited image-study sample is reported. Figure 5 is a pie-chart presentation and does not supply the Table 5 means or inferential statistics (p. 20).

outcomes.name: Article-usage error rate
outcomes.measure_detail: The Error Analysis Coding System identifies grammar, vocabulary, spelling, and logic errors (p. 8, section 3.4). Figure 1 reports error rates within fixed linguistic-error categories. This does not measure numbers of ideas, categories, or unique ideas as required by the codebook category_count definition. The paper does not identify an error coder or a computational scoring procedure, so measure=null. Coder identity, denominator, reliability, participant/text counts, and aggregation are not reported. The displayed aggregate rates do not establish the unit of the underlying analysis, so unit=null rather than assuming output or set. AI availability during the specific test texts is also unstated; question and ai_available_when_produced are null. Lower raw error rates indicate better language accuracy; direction records the reported rate change. Figure values were checked visually in an in-memory render of PDF p. 17. The percentage reduction is also stated in the prose (p. 12, section 5.1.2).

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 remains unclear: section 3.2 explicitly says students were randomly assigned but also calls the design quasi-experimental and describes two natural classes, without explaining allocation or its relationship to class membership (p. 7; p. 15, section 6.3). The assignment checker confirms the literal randomization claim, but the source does not resolve this conflict; field_rct, randomized=yes, and unit=individual remain provisional records of that claim. Criterion 2 remains unclear: 60 students and 30 per group are the stated sampling/assignment counts, and no analyzed people count or attrition information confirms at least 50 analyzed participants (p. 7, section 3.2; p. 8, sections 3.3-3.5; pp. 11-13, results). The 30 works in Table 5 are outputs, not people (p. 13). Criterion 3 is met: creativity is explicitly scored on AI-assisted texts (p. 12, section 5.2.1 and Table 4), with dual teacher scoring and AI cross-validation described on p. 8, section 3.4. Core eligibility is unclear until the allocation procedure and analyzed participant counts are established. context_class=none records that no context class is confirmed: the Table 5 image-source labels do not establish an unassisted-human-versus-AI comparison, because production conditions are unspecified and students used image-generation assistance during instruction (p. 10, section 4.2.4; pp. 12-13, section 5.2.2). No across-person diversity outcome or explicitly AI-withdrawn assessment is established.

one_line_finding: The creativity composite rises from 5.5 pretest to 7.0 posttest (printed +27.3%), but the table supplies no instructional-arm comparison, analyzed people count, or statistical uncertainty (p. 12, Table 4).
open_questions: What was the allocation procedure, and how did individual random assignment relate to the two natural classes and the quasi-experimental label (p. 7, section 3.2)?
How many students were analyzed in each arm and outcome, and were any excluded or missing at posttest (pp. 7-8, 11-13)?

Which instructional group or subset underlies the pretest/posttest means and error distributions, and where are the control-arm results and planned SDs, t-tests, and ANOVAs (p. 8, section 3.5; pp. 11-12; p. 17, Figure 1)?
Was AI allowed during the language posttests and error-analysis texts, and are the creativity texts in section 5.2.1 the Week 8 posttests or instructional products (pp. 8, 11-12)?
What does each duplicated Syntactic Complexity row represent, and are they distinct measures, a labeling error, or conflicting reports of the same measure (p. 11, Table 2)?

What scoring procedures and assessors produced the image metrics, how are the 30 works allocated across sources and students, and what assistance produced the student-image pool (p. 13, section 5.2.2 and Table 5)?
Were the error rates analyzed per text, per participant, or as pooled corpus rates, and what denominators and coding procedures were used (p. 8, Table 1; p. 12, section 5.1.2; p. 17, Figure 1)?

open_items.item: open_questions[0]: What was the allocation procedure, and how did individual random assignment relate to the two natural classes and the quasi-experimental label (p. 7, section 3.2)? Affects criterion 1. An allocation record must explain the randomization procedure, assignment unit, and relationship to the two natural classes.

open_questions[1]: How many students were analyzed in each arm and outcome, and were any excluded or missing at posttest (pp. 7-8, 11-13)? Affects criterion 2. Analyzed student totals by arm and outcome, with exclusions and missing posttests, must establish whether at least 50 distinct people were analyzed.

open_questions[2]: Which instructional group or subset underlies the pretest/posttest means and error distributions, and where are the control-arm results and planned SDs, t-tests, and ANOVAs (p. 8, section 3.5; pp. 11-12; p. 17, Figure 1)? Needed for effect extraction: identify which groups contributed the means and error rates and supply control-group results and uncertainty. Eligibility denominators are addressed by the separate analyzed-count item; missing arm estimates alone do not change the three criteria.

open_questions[3]: Was AI allowed during the language posttests and error-analysis texts, and are the creativity texts in section 5.2.1 the Week 8 posttests or instructional products (pp. 8, 11-12)? Needed for with_ai versus after_ai and test-versus-coursework classification. Criterion 3 is independently supported by the explicitly scored AI-assisted creativity texts; authors must state test instructions and the relationship of Table 4 texts to the Week 8 assessments.

open_questions[4]: What does each duplicated Syntactic Complexity row represent, and are they distinct measures, a labeling error, or conflicting reports of the same measure (p. 11, Table 2)? Needed for outcome identity and extraction. Authors must identify each duplicated Table 2 row or correct its label; the scored-creativity eligibility criterion is already met.

open_questions[5]: What scoring procedures and assessors produced the image metrics, how are the 30 works allocated across sources and students, and what assistance produced the student-image pool (p. 13, section 5.2.2 and Table 5)? Needed for image coding and any context classification. Authors must identify image assessors and scoring rules, map the works to students and sources, identify who prompted the AI images, and describe assistance for the student-image pool. The text-creativity outcomes already establish criterion 3.

open_questions[6]: Were the error rates analyzed per text, per participant, or as pooled corpus rates, and what denominators and coding procedures were used (p. 8, Table 1; p. 12, section 5.1.2; p. 17, Figure 1)? Needed for error-outcome measurement and analysis units. Authors must give the coding procedure, denominators, coder identity, aggregation, and underlying observations; text-creativity scoring already establishes criterion 3.

open_questions[7]: How do the conclusion creativity values of 3.4 and 4.6 out of 5 and writing increase of 12.6% relate to the different values in Tables 4 and 2 (pp. 11-12, 14)?
